title: Vector Database Systems in Practice
description: Qdrant, managed services like Pinecone, and pgvector as concrete instances of the decision framework from Module 0.

lessons.title: Qdrant in Practice
lessons.description: A concrete look at one popular purpose-built vector database, as a representative of the category.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Describe Qdrant's core concepts — collections, points, and payloads — and where it fits among your options.

sections.title: 📦 Collections and points
sections.content: Qdrant organizes vectors into collections (similar to a table), where each entry is a 'point' — a vector plus its payload metadata and a unique ID. Collections are configured with a distance metric and vector size upfront, so the normalization lesson from Module 0 directly determines how you configure a real collection.

sections.title: 🔎 Filtering is a first-class feature
sections.content: Qdrant's filter syntax supports the tenant/access-control patterns from Module 2 directly — combining a vector search with must/should/must_not conditions on payload fields in a single query, rather than filtering after the fact in application code.

sections.title: 🐳 Operationally
sections.content: Qdrant can run self-hosted (as a Docker container, matching the containerization patterns from the Cloud course) or as a managed cloud service — the self-hosted-vs-managed decision from Module 0's 'choosing a vector database' lesson made concrete for one specific product.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Filtering after retrieval instead of inside the query.** Qdrant's must/should/must_not filters run inside the vector search itself; running the tenant/access check in application code afterward means paying for irrelevant vectors and rows you'll just throw away.

**Changing the distance metric after data is already indexed.** Since a collection's metric and vector size are fixed at creation, switching to a different metric mid-flight means the existing index no longer matches — the collection has to be recreated and re-populated, not patched in place.

**Assuming self-hosted and managed Qdrant behave identically operationally.** The query API and filter syntax are the same, but who handles upgrades, backups, and scaling differs completely — treating the deployment choice as a detail rather than the Module 0 decision it actually is.

questions.question: In Qdrant, a 'point' represents
options: A single vector plus its payload metadata and unique ID
An entire collection of vectors
A distance metric configuration
A sharding rule
questions.explanation: A point is the basic unit stored in a Qdrant collection: one vector, its metadata, and an ID.

questions.question: Why does Qdrant require a distance metric to be configured when a collection is created?
options: Because the collection's search behavior depends on it, connecting directly to the normalization/metric choice from earlier in this course
Because Qdrant only supports one metric globally, never per collection
Because distance metrics can be changed per-query with no other configuration
Because Qdrant does not support cosine similarity
questions.explanation: Collections are configured with a specific metric and vector size upfront, which is why the earlier metric-choice lesson matters when actually setting one up.

questions.question: Qdrant's filter syntax lets you
options: Combine vector search with must/should/must_not conditions on payload fields in a single query
Only filter after retrieving all results in application code
Search without specifying a vector at all
Automatically detect tenant boundaries without configuration
questions.explanation: Native filter support means the tenant-isolation and metadata-filtering patterns from earlier lessons can be expressed directly in the query itself.

questions.question: Per the lesson, the choice between running Qdrant self-hosted or as a managed cloud service is best described as
options: A concrete instance of the self-hosted-vs-managed decision introduced in Module 0's 'choosing a vector database' lesson
A choice that has no connection to anything covered earlier in the course
Something Qdrant does not actually support — only self-hosting is possible
A decision that only affects payload filtering, not deployment
questions.explanation: The lesson frames Qdrant's self-hosted-vs-managed option as the Module 0 decision framework made concrete for one specific product.

questions.question: What two properties are configured on a Qdrant collection when it is first created?
options: Vector size and distance metric
Tenant ID and access-control role
CPU count and disk size
Payload schema and API key
questions.explanation: The lesson states collections are configured with a distance metric and vector size upfront.

questions.question: In the toy make_collection_config function, what happens if you pass a distance value that is not 'Cosine', 'Euclid', or 'Dot'?
options: It raises a ValueError instead of silently accepting the unsupported metric
It defaults silently to 'Cosine'
It stores the value as-is with no validation
It deletes the collection if one already exists
questions.explanation: make_collection_config checks distance against the tuple of supported values and raises ValueError for anything else.

questions.question: In the toy make_search_request function, what causes the returned request's filter dict to include a 'must' key?
options: Passing a truthy value for the must argument
Setting top_k to a value greater than 10
Passing a query_vector with more than three numbers
It always includes 'must', regardless of arguments
questions.explanation: The function only adds request['filter']['must'] = must inside the `if must:` branch, so it only appears when a truthy must argument is passed.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is filtering after retrieval instead of inside the query considered a mistake?
options: Because it means paying the cost of fetching irrelevant vectors and rows that get thrown away, instead of letting the native filter narrow the search itself
Because Qdrant does not allow any filtering after retrieval under any circumstances
Because application-code filtering always returns incorrect results
Because must/should/must_not conditions can only be used at collection-creation time
questions.explanation: The mistakes section explains that native filters run inside the vector search itself, so filtering afterward in application code wastes work on vectors you discard anyway.

lessons.title: Pinecone and Managed Services
lessons.description: What you gain — and give up — by letting someone else run the index.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: List the operational trade-offs of a fully managed vector search service compared to self-hosting.

sections.title: ☁️ What managed buys you
sections.content: A managed service like Pinecone handles sharding, replication, scaling, and upgrades for you — the operational lessons from Module 3 (backups, monitoring, cost control) are largely the vendor's problem rather than yours, in exchange for a subscription cost and less low-level control.

sections.title: 🔒 What you give up
sections.content: Less control over exact index parameters, data residency constraints (your vectors live on the vendor's infrastructure, which may matter for the compliance concerns the Eval & Security course raised about data handling), and a dependency on the vendor's uptime and roadmap rather than your own.

sections.title: 🧮 When it makes sense
sections.content: For a small team without dedicated infrastructure expertise, or a product where time-to-market matters more than fine-grained cost or configuration control, managed services remove an entire category of operational work. For a large-scale system with strict data residency or cost requirements, self-hosting often becomes worth the added operational burden.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
A toy cost/throughput estimator for a managed vector-service "pod" configuration:

```python
# A toy cost/throughput estimator for a managed vector-service "pod"
# configuration (illustrative numbers only, not any real vendor's pricing).

POD_CATALOG = {
    "s1": {"vectors_per_pod": 5_000_000, "qps_per_pod": 20, "cost_per_hour": 0.10},
    "p1": {"vectors_per_pod": 1_000_000, "qps_per_pod": 100, "cost_per_hour": 0.40},
    "p2": {"vectors_per_pod": 1_000_000, "qps_per_pod": 200, "cost_per_hour": 0.80},
}


def estimate_pods_needed(pod_type, total_vectors, target_qps):
    spec = POD_CATALOG[pod_type]
    pods_for_storage = -(-total_vectors // spec["vectors_per_pod"])  # ceiling division
    pods_for_throughput = -(-target_qps // spec["qps_per_pod"])
    return max(pods_for_storage, pods_for_throughput)


def estimate_monthly_cost(pod_type, total_vectors, target_qps, hours_per_month=730):
    pods = estimate_pods_needed(pod_type, total_vectors, target_qps)
    spec = POD_CATALOG[pod_type]
    return pods * spec["cost_per_hour"] * hours_per_month


for pod_type in ("s1", "p1", "p2"):
    pods = estimate_pods_needed(pod_type, total_vectors=8_000_000, target_qps=150)
    cost = estimate_monthly_cost(pod_type, total_vectors=8_000_000, target_qps=150)
    print(f"{pod_type}: {pods} pods, ~${cost:.2f}/month")
```

Notice that `estimate_pods_needed` takes the *max* of the pods required for storage and the pods required for throughput, not the sum — a deployment sized for only one of the two would be under-provisioned on the other. Changing `pod_type` changes both the storage-per-pod and throughput-per-pod numbers at once, the same way choosing a different managed tier changes both dimensions of a real deployment together.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Sizing a managed deployment for storage alone, ignoring query throughput.** A pod configuration that comfortably holds your vector count can still fall over under real query volume if it wasn't sized for QPS too.

**Treating the managed subscription price as the full cost comparison.** The subscription fee against self-hosting's server cost is only part of the comparison; the engineering time a managed service saves (or a self-hosted system consumes) belongs in the same comparison from Module 0.

**Assuming data residency is automatically satisfied by picking a nearby cloud region.** A managed vendor's regional options can still fall short of specific compliance requirements (data never leaving a particular jurisdiction, specific certifications) — that needs to be checked against the actual requirement, not assumed.

questions.question: A key advantage of a managed vector search service is that it
options: Handles operational concerns like sharding, replication, and scaling on your behalf
Always costs less than self-hosting at any scale
Removes the need for any distance metric configuration
Guarantees perfect recall regardless of settings
questions.explanation: Offloading operational work — the exact concerns covered in the operating-at-scale module — is the core value proposition of a managed service.

questions.question: A potential downside of a managed vector search service is
options: Reduced control over data residency and low-level index configuration
Inability to store metadata payloads
Inability to perform any vector search at all
A requirement to self-host the embedding model
questions.explanation: Handing operations to a vendor typically means less control over where data lives and exactly how the index is tuned.

questions.question: A managed vector service is often the better choice when
options: A team lacks dedicated infrastructure expertise and time-to-market matters more than fine-grained control
Strict data residency requirements rule out third-party hosting
Cost must be minimized at massive scale above all else
The team wants full control over every index parameter
questions.explanation: The trade favors managed services when operational simplicity outweighs the value of granular control — the reverse conditions favor self-hosting.

questions.question: Per the lesson, which of the following is explicitly listed as something a managed service like Pinecone handles for you?
options: Sharding, replication, scaling, and upgrades
Choosing which embedding model your application uses
Writing your application's business logic
Designing your product's user interface
questions.explanation: The lesson names sharding, replication, scaling, and upgrades as the operational work a managed service takes on for you.

questions.question: Per the lesson, self-hosting often becomes worth the added operational burden when
options: A large-scale system has strict data residency or cost requirements
The team has no infrastructure expertise at all
Time-to-market matters more than anything else
The product is still an early, unvalidated prototype
questions.explanation: The lesson states that for a large-scale system with strict data residency or cost requirements, self-hosting often becomes worth the added operational burden.

questions.question: In the estimator code, why does estimate_pods_needed take the max of pods_for_storage and pods_for_throughput rather than their sum?
options: Because a single pod provides both storage and query capacity at once, so you need enough pods to satisfy whichever requirement demands more, not both added together
Because pods_for_throughput is always larger and the other value is unused
Because Python's // operator forces the use of max in this context
Because the sum would always equal zero for these inputs
questions.explanation: Each pod already contributes to both storage and throughput capacity simultaneously, so the binding constraint is whichever requirement needs more pods — not the two added together.

questions.question: For pod type 's1' (vectors_per_pod=5,000,000) in the code, how many pods does the storage requirement alone need for total_vectors=8,000,000?
options: 2, since ceiling(8,000,000 / 5,000,000) rounds 1.6 up to 2
1, since 8,000,000 is close enough to 5,000,000
8, one pod per million vectors
0, because 8,000,000 is below the pod's capacity
questions.explanation: pods_for_storage uses ceiling division, and 8,000,000 / 5,000,000 = 1.6, which rounds up to 2 pods.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is sizing a managed deployment for storage alone risky?
options: Because a deployment that comfortably holds the vector count can still fail under real query throughput if it wasn't sized for QPS too
Because storage-only sizing always overestimates the number of pods needed
Because managed services do not track query throughput at all
Because storage capacity and query throughput are always identical for every pod type
questions.explanation: The mistakes section warns that ignoring throughput when sizing can leave a deployment that holds the data but can't sustain real query load.

lessons.title: pgvector: Postgres as a Vector Store
lessons.description: Sometimes the right vector database is the relational database you're already running.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain when adding vector search to an existing Postgres database is preferable to a dedicated vector database.

sections.title: 🐘 One system instead of two
sections.content: pgvector is a Postgres extension that adds a vector column type and index types (including HNSW and IVFFlat) directly inside Postgres. This means vector search can live in the same database as your relational data — joined in the same SQL query as the tables you built in the SQL course — instead of syncing data between two separate systems.

sections.title: ⚖️ The trade-off: simplicity for ceiling
sections.content: pgvector's HNSW implementation is generally solid but tends to have a lower practical scale ceiling and fewer specialized features (like the rich payload filtering of Qdrant) than a purpose-built vector database. For a system already running Postgres with a moderate number of vectors, it removes an entire system from your architecture; for a system needing billions of vectors or extremely low query latency at massive concurrency, a dedicated system usually wins.

sections.title: 🔗 A SQL-native way to think about hybrid search
sections.content: Because pgvector search happens inside normal SQL, combining a vector similarity search with the exact-match filters or joins from the SQL course's window-functions and joins lessons is often more natural than in a standalone vector database — you're writing one SQL query instead of coordinating two systems' query languages.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
A toy function that builds a parameterized pgvector-style SQL query string with a metadata WHERE clause:

```python
# A toy function that builds a parameterized pgvector-style SQL query
# string (illustrative — no real database driver involved).

def build_similarity_query(table, vector_column, embedding, top_k=10, filters=None):
    filters = filters or {}
    where_clauses = []
    params = []

    for column, value in filters.items():
        where_clauses.append(f"{column} = %s")
        params.append(value)

    where_sql = ""
    if where_clauses:
        where_sql = "WHERE " + " AND ".join(where_clauses) + "\n"

    query = (
        f"SELECT id, {vector_column} <-> %s AS distance\n"
        f"FROM {table}\n"
        f"{where_sql}"
        f"ORDER BY distance\n"
        f"LIMIT %s;"
    )

    params = [embedding] + params + [top_k]
    return query, params


query, params = build_similarity_query(
    table="documents",
    vector_column="embedding",
    embedding=[0.1, 0.2, 0.3],
    top_k=5,
    filters={"tenant_id": "acme_corp", "status": "published"},
)

print(query)
print(params)
```

Notice that `<->` (pgvector's distance operator) sits inside the same `SELECT` / `WHERE` / `ORDER BY` / `LIMIT` statement as the ordinary `tenant_id` and `status` filters — one SQL query, not two systems being coordinated — and that `params` keeps the embedding, filter values, and `top_k` positionally aligned with each `%s` placeholder.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Interpolating filter values directly into the SQL string instead of using parameters.** Building the WHERE clause with f-string value interpolation (rather than placeholders and a params list) opens the door to SQL injection — exactly the kind of mistake a `%s` placeholder is meant to prevent.

**Forgetting to build an index (HNSW/IVFFlat) on the vector column.** Without one, pgvector falls back to a full sequential scan comparing every row, which erases most of the performance benefit and can silently make queries much slower as the table grows.

**Expecting pgvector to match a purpose-built vector database's filtering features one-for-one.** SQL WHERE clauses cover simple equality/range filters well, but the rich must/should/must_not filter combinators of a dedicated vector database (like Qdrant) aren't something pgvector replicates.

questions.question: The main architectural benefit of pgvector is that it
options: Lets vector search live in the same database as relational data, avoiding syncing between two separate systems
Eliminates the need for any distance metric
Only works for sparse vectors
Provides better scale than any purpose-built vector database
questions.explanation: Keeping vectors inside Postgres means one system and one query language instead of coordinating data across two databases.

questions.question: Compared to a purpose-built vector database, pgvector generally
options: Has a lower practical scale ceiling and fewer specialized features, in exchange for architectural simplicity
Always scales better at billions of vectors
Cannot be combined with SQL joins or filters
Requires a completely separate query language
questions.explanation: pgvector trades some scale and specialized feature depth for the simplicity of staying inside a database you already run.

questions.question: Why might combining vector search with a SQL join feel more natural in pgvector than in a standalone vector database?
options: Because both the vector search and the relational filter/join happen within the same SQL query and system
Because standalone vector databases cannot use any metadata at all
Because pgvector does not support the WHERE clause
Because SQL cannot express similarity search under any circumstances
questions.explanation: A single SQL query spanning both vector similarity and relational conditions avoids coordinating two separate systems' query interfaces.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which index types does pgvector add to Postgres for vector columns?
options: HNSW and IVFFlat
B-tree and hash indexes only
A proprietary index type unrelated to any algorithm discussed elsewhere in the course
No index types — pgvector always performs a full table scan
questions.explanation: The lesson states pgvector adds a vector column type and index types including HNSW and IVFFlat directly inside Postgres.

questions.question: Per the lesson, for a system already running Postgres with a moderate number of vectors, what does adopting pgvector remove from the architecture?
options: An entire separate system that would otherwise need to be run and kept in sync
The need for any relational tables at all
The requirement to ever write SQL
The concept of a distance metric
questions.explanation: The lesson says that for a moderate-scale system already on Postgres, pgvector removes an entire system from the architecture.

questions.question: In build_similarity_query, what is the purpose of the params list returned alongside the query string?
options: It holds the embedding, filter values, and top_k in the same order as the query's %s placeholders, for safe parameterized execution
It stores the names of the SQL columns being selected
It counts how many rows the query is expected to return
It is unused — the function only returns it for logging purposes
questions.explanation: params is built as [embedding] + filter values + [top_k], matching the positional order of the %s placeholders in the query string.

questions.question: Given filters={"tenant_id": "acme_corp", "status": "published"}, what does the generated WHERE clause look like?
options: WHERE tenant_id = %s AND status = %s
WHERE tenant_id == acme_corp OR status == published
WHERE tenant_id IN (acme_corp, published)
No WHERE clause is generated when filters are provided
questions.explanation: The loop over filters.items() appends one 'column = %s' clause per filter and joins them with AND, producing 'WHERE tenant_id = %s AND status = %s'.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is interpolating filter values directly into a SQL string dangerous?
options: It opens the door to SQL injection, which parameterized %s placeholders are designed to prevent
It makes the query run slower than using an index
It causes pgvector to ignore the vector column entirely
It is not actually dangerous, only a stylistic issue
questions.explanation: The mistakes section explains that building the WHERE clause via direct string interpolation (instead of parameters) creates a SQL injection risk.

lessons.title: Choosing Self-Hosted vs. Managed
lessons.description: Bringing Module 0's decision framework back with real products in view.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Apply the decision framework from Module 0 to a concrete self-hosted-vs-managed choice, now that you've seen specific systems.

sections.title: 🔁 Revisit the original questions with real options
sections.content: Scale: Qdrant self-hosted or a managed service both handle large scale, but at different operational cost. Update pattern and filtering: pgvector's simplicity might suffice if your relational data and vector needs overlap heavily. Operational model: a small team leans managed; a team with existing infrastructure expertise and cost sensitivity leans self-hosted.

sections.title: 🧾 A worked example
sections.content: A three-person startup building a RAG-powered support tool with under a million documents: pgvector inside their existing Postgres, or a managed service, both avoid taking on infrastructure work they don't have the headcount for. A large enterprise with 500 million documents, strict data residency requirements, and a dedicated platform team: self-hosted Qdrant or Milvus, run inside their own infrastructure, matches both the scale and the compliance need.

sections.title: 🚪 The decision is reversible, mostly
sections.content: Migrating vector databases later is real work — re-embedding is usually not required if you kept your embeddings, but reindexing and cutover need planning — so it's not a decision to treat as permanent, but it's also not free to change, which is one more reason the requirements-first approach from Module 0 pays off before committing.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Scoring criteria on inconsistent scales (some "higher is better", some "lower is better") without normalizing them first.** Mixing the two inside one weighted sum silently rewards the wrong option unless every criterion is put on the same "higher is better" scale first.

**Picking weights that don't reflect the team's actual priorities, then treating the resulting score as objective.** A weighted score is only as good as the weights behind it — quietly defaulting to equal weights (or copying someone else's) bakes in priorities that may not match the requirements-first approach Module 0 recommends.

**Treating the decision as permanent because switching feels risky.** The lesson notes migration is real work but not impossible — re-embedding usually isn't required — so avoiding a review of the decision out of migration-anxiety can leave a team stuck with a mismatch.

questions.question: For a small team with limited infrastructure expertise building a modest-scale RAG tool, which factor most favors a managed service or pgvector?
options: Avoiding operational work the team doesn't have the headcount to do well
The need for petabyte-scale storage
A strict requirement for on-premises data residency
The need for custom low-level index tuning
questions.explanation: Limited operational capacity is exactly the condition that favors offloading infrastructure work, whether via a managed service or the simplicity of pgvector.

questions.question: A large enterprise with strict data residency requirements and 500 million documents would most likely lean toward
options: Self-hosted infrastructure like Qdrant or Milvus run within their own environment
A fully managed public cloud vector service with no residency guarantees
Storing all vectors in a spreadsheet
Avoiding vector search entirely
questions.explanation: Residency and scale requirements at that level typically require infrastructure the organization controls directly.

questions.question: Why is migrating vector databases described as 'not free to change' even though embeddings themselves can often be reused?
options: Because reindexing and cutover to a new system still require real planning and execution work
Because embeddings always become invalid when switching databases
Because vector database migrations are illegal without vendor approval
Because migration always requires retraining the embedding model
questions.explanation: Even without re-embedding, moving a live index to a new system involves nontrivial reindexing and cutover work.

questions.question: Per the lesson's revisit of the original decision questions, what most determines whether a team leans self-hosted rather than managed, aside from scale?
options: Whether the team has existing infrastructure expertise and is cost sensitive
Whether the team's product has a logo yet
Whether the team prefers a particular programming language
Whether the team has ever used a spreadsheet before
questions.explanation: The lesson states that a team with existing infrastructure expertise and cost sensitivity leans self-hosted, while a small team leans managed.

questions.question: In the worked example, what did both of the three-person startup's options (pgvector or a managed service) have in common?
options: Both avoided taking on infrastructure work the team didn't have the headcount for
Both required hiring a dedicated platform team first
Both required strict data residency guarantees
Both required 500 million documents to be cost-effective
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that for the small startup, either pgvector or a managed service avoids infrastructure work they lack the headcount to do.

questions.question: In the toy weighted_score function, what does raising a criterion's weight in CRITERIA_WEIGHTS do to the final ranking?
options: It increases that criterion's influence on each option's total score, which can change which option ranks first
It removes that criterion from the calculation entirely
It has no effect unless the option's score for that criterion is also changed
It automatically normalizes all other weights to zero
questions.explanation: weighted_score multiplies each criterion's score by its weight and sums them, so a larger weight gives that criterion more influence over the total — and potentially the ranking.

questions.question: Why is operational_burden scored so that a higher number means less burden, per the code's comment?
options: So that every criterion in the weighted sum consistently follows a 'higher score is better' convention
Because Python requires all dictionary values to be positive
Because operational_burden is not actually used in weighted_score
So that the option with the most burden always wins the ranking
questions.explanation: The comment flags that a higher operational_burden score means less burden, keeping it on the same 'higher is better' scale as the other criteria so the weighted sum stays meaningful.

questions.question: Per 'Common mistakes', why is mixing 'higher is better' and 'lower is better' criteria in one weighted sum a problem?
options: It silently rewards the wrong option unless every criterion is normalized to the same direction first
It causes a runtime error whenever the score is calculated
It only matters if there are more than ten criteria
It has no real effect on which option scores highest
questions.explanation: The mistakes section warns that mixing scale directions without normalizing first can make the weighted sum favor an option it shouldn't.
